title: Influence of Arabic and Islamic Philosophy on Judaic Thought

summaries.example: Imagine a student reading a science book, then explaining one idea in a new language and using it in a different project. That is somewhat like what happened when Jewish thinkers read Arabic philosophical works, had them translated into Hebrew, and used some ideas in their own discussions. They did not all agree, and a later writer may have learned an idea through another Jewish author rather than from the original book.
summaries.summary: This entry explains how philosophy written in Arabic, including works by Muslim and Christian authors, reached medieval Jewish thinkers. The exchange happened through reading, translation, quotation, commentary, and adaptation. Some Jewish writers used ideas from al-Kindi, al-Farabi, Avicenna, al-Ghazali, Ibn Bajja, Ibn Tufayl, Averroes, and others. The strongest evidence concerns particular books and ideas, not a single simple story. For example, al-Farabi shaped Jewish studies of logic and knowledge, while Averroes became a major guide to Aristotle for many later Jewish philosophers. The entry also warns that a Jewish author may have learned an idea indirectly, perhaps through Maimonides or another writer. It therefore treats “influence” as something that needs careful evidence.
key_ideas: Jewish thinkers in the Middle Ages sometimes learned from Arabic and Islamic philosophers.
Ideas traveled through original Arabic works, Hebrew translations, and the writings of other Jewish thinkers.
Arabic philosophy and Islamic philosophy overlap, but they are not exactly the same thing.
Scholars can prove some connections, while other possible connections remain uncertain.
Averroes, al-Farabi, Avicenna, al-Ghazali, and other thinkers were important sources in different ways.
summaries.why_it_matters: This history shows that learning often travels across languages, communities, and religious traditions. It also teaches us to be careful: finding similar ideas does not always prove that one author copied or directly read another. Studying translations and commentaries helps us see how people made older ideas useful for new questions.

important_terms.definition: The study of big questions about knowledge, reality, nature, God, and how people should live.
A connection between an earlier thinker’s work and a later thinker’s ideas. Scholars use this word carefully and look for evidence.
Changing writing from one language into another so readers of the new language can understand it.
A medieval Jewish language written with Hebrew letters and used by Jewish communities in Arabic-speaking places.

summaries.example: Suppose a student studies Aristotle through three layers: an Arabic philosopher’s interpretation, a Hebrew translation, and a later Jewish commentary. If the final text shares a distinctive argument with the earlier work, scholars may investigate influence. But they must ask whether the Jewish author read the Arabic original, used a Hebrew translation, or learned the point through an intermediary such as Maimonides. Similarity alone is not enough.
summaries.summary: The entry surveys how medieval Jewish thinkers encountered and employed philosophical materials associated with Arabic- and Islamic-world authors from roughly the tenth through fifteenth centuries. Its central methodological point is that “influence” should normally mean a direct and evidential use of a source, not merely a resemblance between doctrines. The evidence includes translations, identifiable quotations, adapted definitions, commentaries, encyclopedias, and arguments built from earlier works. Al-Kindi’s impact appears limited but visible in figures such as Isaac Israeli. The Brethren of Purity influenced Jewish treatments of cosmology, the soul, science, and the human being as a microcosm. Al-Farabi was especially important for logic and the classification of knowledge. Avicenna and al-Ghazali supplied materials for attempts to relate philosophy to religious tradition, though scholars debate how directly Maimonides and others knew them. Ibn Bajja and Ibn Tufayl had more focused effects. Averroes’s commentaries on Aristotle were translated extensively into Hebrew and became central to later Jewish philosophical study, producing both loyal followers and critics. Christian Arabic authors and works such as the Arabic De causis also contributed to this complex network. The entry repeatedly notes that many proposed links remain tentative or require further study.
key_ideas: The entry is not a complete history of every connection between Arabic-Islamic philosophy and Judaic thought; it focuses on cases where evidence is available or especially important.
Transmission occurred through Arabic originals, Judeo-Arabic texts, Hebrew translations, Latin versions, quotations, abridgments, and commentaries.
Al-Farabi strongly affected Jewish work in logic, classification of the sciences, ethics, metaphysics, and the relation between philosophy and religion.
Avicenna and al-Ghazali often reached Jewish thinkers indirectly, and Jewish authors frequently combined their ideas with those of other philosophers.
Averroes became a particularly important interpreter of Aristotle, although Jewish philosophers differed in how faithfully or critically they followed him.
The entry distinguishes direct influence from resemblance, possible influence, and influence transmitted through an intermediary.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters because it challenges a picture of Jewish, Islamic, and Christian intellectual history as isolated traditions. It shows a multilingual chain of transmission in which ideas were translated, selected, reinterpreted, and sometimes used against their original authors’ positions. It also models responsible historical reasoning: scholars must distinguish direct borrowing, indirect transmission, shared inheritance, and later reconstruction.

important_terms.definition: A historical relation in which a later author directly and demonstrably employs an earlier source, whether by quotation, translation, commentary, or substantive use.
A philosophical tradition written in Arabic; it includes Muslim authors, but also some Christian authors who wrote in Arabic, and it is not identical with Islamic philosophy.
Philosophical writing connected with Islam; some important Islamic works were written in Persian, so the category is broader than Arabic philosophy.
A medieval Jewish language that used Arabic vocabulary and was written in Hebrew script.
A form of philosophical writing that explains, analyzes, or responds to an earlier text rather than merely repeating it.
A position associated with Avicenna, especially one that uses elements of his philosophy in discussing religion and philosophy; medieval Jewish authors often used such ideas selectively.
A medieval movement or tendency among Jewish thinkers who used al-Ghazali’s philosophical and theological works, sometimes to support religious tradition or criticize Averroist positions.
The use of Averroes’s interpretations of Aristotle by later Jewish philosophers, especially through Hebrew translations and supercommentaries.

summaries.example: Think of a group project about how the solar system works. One student reads a book in Arabic, another translates parts into Hebrew, and a third explains the ideas in a new encyclopedia. A later student might learn from the encyclopedia without ever seeing the first book. Historians face a similar problem when tracing medieval philosophy: they must find out not only whether two ideas resemble each other, but also how the idea traveled.
summaries.summary: This entry studies the many ways Arabic, Islamic, and some Christian Arabic philosophers affected medieval Judaic thought. The story is a network, not a one-way transfer. Jewish thinkers encountered works in Arabic, Judeo-Arabic, Hebrew translation, and sometimes Latin. They might quote a passage, reshape a definition, write a commentary, or use an argument in a new discussion. The entry examines al-Kindi, Abu Bakr al-Razi, the Brethren of Purity, al-Farabi, Avicenna, al-Ghazali, Ibn Bajja, Ibn Tufayl, Averroes, later Avicennian writers, and Christian Arabic authors. Al-Farabi had a broad effect on Jewish logic and on the study of knowledge. Avicenna and al-Ghazali offered ideas that some Jewish authors used when trying to relate philosophy to religious tradition. Averroes’s commentaries on Aristotle were translated into Hebrew and read widely, helping create Jewish Averroism, though some later thinkers challenged it. The entry stresses that not every resemblance proves influence. A Jewish philosopher might have learned an idea indirectly, and several thinkers may have contributed to the same tradition.
key_ideas: Medieval Jewish philosophy developed in conversation with Arabic and Islamic philosophy, rather than in isolation.
The exchange happened through reading, translating, quoting, summarizing, commenting, and adapting.
Al-Farabi was influential in logic, the organization of the sciences, ethics, and questions about philosophy and religion.
Avicenna and al-Ghazali influenced Jewish authors in different and sometimes indirect ways.
Averroes became one of the most important guides to Aristotle for later Jewish philosophers, especially after his works were translated into Hebrew.
The evidence is uneven: some links are clear, while others are only possible and are still debated by scholars.
summaries.why_it_matters: The subject helps explain how intellectual traditions grow through contact. It also shows why historians need more than lists of similar ideas: they trace languages, translations, quotations, and the paths by which books were read. This makes the history both richer and more careful.

important_terms.definition: A way of thinking about questions such as what exists, how we know things, and how people should live.
A supported connection in which a later writer used an earlier work or idea, directly or through a traceable route.
A version of a work in another language. Medieval Jewish scholars often encountered Arabic philosophy through Hebrew translations.
A writing that explains, evaluates, or develops another author’s work.
Philosophy written in Arabic. It included Muslim thinkers and also some Christian writers, so it is not exactly the same as Islamic philosophy.
Philosophy connected with Islamic intellectual traditions. Some Islamic philosophical works were written in Persian as well as Arabic.
A philosophical tendency linked with Averroes, especially the use of his explanations of Aristotle in later Jewish thought.
A tendency among some Jewish thinkers to use al-Ghazali’s works when discussing philosophy and religious tradition.

questions_to_think_about: Why is a direct quotation stronger evidence than a general similarity?
How could a translator become an interpreter, not just a language converter?
Why might Jewish philosophers borrow ideas from a thinker they criticized?
What can a history of translations tell us about who had access to knowledge?
Why does the entry avoid treating all Arabic-speaking or Islamic thinkers as one group?
